### Exercise 3 {-}

Suppose you have arranged for a phone call to be at 3 pm on May 8, 2025 at Arizona time. However, the recipient will be in Auckland, NZ. What time will it be there? 

```{r}
ymd_hm('2025-May-8 3:00 pm', tz='US/Arizona')


ymd_hm('2025-May-8 3:00 pm', tz='NZ')
```
Arizona is UTC -7 and NZ is UTC +12 or +13 depending on time of the year. Because this is in May it would push the time forward one hour making it UTC +13. Arizona time relative to UTC is 2025-May-8 8:00 am. NZ relative to UTC is 2025-May-9 4:00 am.

### Exercise 4 {-}

From this book's [GitHub](https://github.com/BuscagliaR/STA_444_v2/) directory, navigate to the `data-raw` directory and then download the `Pulliam_Airport_Weather_Station.csv` data file. (*There are several weather station files. Make sure you get the correct one!*)  There is a `DATE` column (is it of type `date` when you import the data?) as well as the Maximum and Minimum temperature. For the last 5 years of data included in the file, plot the time series of daily maximum temperature with date on the x-axis. Write your code so that it will work if I update the date set. *Hint: Find the maximum date in the data set and then subtract 5 years. Will there be a difference if you use `dyears(5)` vs `years(5)`? Which seems more appropriate here?*

```{r}
df <- read.csv("data-raw/Pulliam_Airport_Weather_Station.csv")
```


```{r}
#check the type of the column
class(df$DATE)
```
Date is of type character.

```{r, include =FALSE}

# get the maximum date in the df
max_date <- max(df$DATE)

# change it to a date type
max_date <- as.Date(max_date)

class(max_date)
```

To subtract 5 years from the maximum date I think we need to use dyears() instead of years because it accounts for discontinuities and gives us a more accurate result.

```{r}
start_date <- (max_date - dyears(5))
```

```{r, fig.width=12, fig.height=8}
# now we want the time series for the 5 year of daily max temp.
# first we need to select the rows that have a date of start_date or more

df_new <- df |> filter(DATE >= start_date)

# now we need to plot time on the x axis and TMAX on the y axis

ggplot(data = df_new, aes(x=DATE, y=TMAX))+
      geom_point()
```

### Exercise 5 {-}

It turns out there is some interesting periodicity regarding the number of births on particular days of the year.

**a)** Using the `mosaicData` package, load the data set `Births78` which records the number of children born on each day in the United States in 1978. Because this problem is intended to show how to calculate the information using the `date`, remove all the columns *except* `date` and `births`.

```{r}
library(mosaicData)

data(Births78)

Births78 <- Births78[, c(1,2)]
```


**b)** Graph the number of `births` vs the `date` with date on the x-axis. What stands out to you? Why do you think we have this trend?

```{r}
ggplot(data=Births78, aes(x=date, y=births))+
      geom_point()
```
The first thing that stands out is that there is a gap in between the points where we could draw a wave. The numbers are either above or below that wave. I am not sure what explains this so I will not comment on that part. However, I do notice that there is an oscillation that happens between the months and the overall trend is upwards. I am not sure why this is the case but if I had to guess I would say the increase is directly correlated with the amount of "free time" the parents have available (9 months prior). If I am right then that would mean the most free time people generally have is around December each year given that the maximum amount of births happen in September.

**c)** To test your assumption, we need to figure out the what day of the week each observation is. Use `dplyr::mutate` to add a new column named `dow` that is the day of the week (Monday, Tuesday, etc). This calculation will involve some function in the `lubridate` package and the `date` column.

```{r}
# we will need this function wday(x, label=TRUE, abbr=FALSE)

Births78 <- Births78 |> mutate(dow = wday(date, label=TRUE, abbr=FALSE))
```


**d)** Plot the data with the point color being determined by the day of the week variable.

```{r}
ggplot(data=Births78, aes(x=date, y=births, colour = dow))+
      geom_point()
```
Looks like my hypothesis was not being tested here. This is actually explaining the gap which exists in the graph. The colors show that this is due to there being a lower number of births on the weekend.
